criteria.title: Three-sided scope, not ride-sharing with food

levels.0: Lists browse and order only, or designs a two-party ride-sharing flow with no restaurant step.
levels.1: Covers browse, checkout, restaurant acceptance, dispatch and tracking, but never says how food preparation time or batching changes the problem.
levels.2: Covers all six flows, names the restaurant as an unreliable third party, and states early that prep time and batching (not nearest driver) shape dispatch.

levels.0: No targets, or only 'fast and scalable'.
levels.1: States latency and availability, but treats 'charge exactly once' and 'never double-book a courier' as afterthoughts.
levels.2: Assignment within 30 s at p99, no double-booking except deliberate batching, exactly-once charging with idempotent refunds, browse p99, tracking freshness vs reliable status delivery, and the predictable 4× meal peaks.

criteria.title: Orders, couriers and pings derived step by step

levels.0: No numbers, or numbers with no derivation.
levels.1: Gets about 58 orders/s and some location rate, but never derives online couriers or the peak.
levels.2: 5M ÷ 86,400 = 57.9/s, 231.5/s at peak; about 1,852 order writes/s at peak; 208,333 orders/h ÷ 2 per courier-hour = 104,167 online, 416,667 at peak; ÷ 5 s = 83,333 pings/s; and concludes pings outnumber order writes about 45 to 1.

criteria.title: Maps and PSP budgets drive the design

levels.0: Calls the maps provider wherever an ETA is shown, with no arithmetic.
levels.1: Notices the maps rate limit but does not quantify browse ETAs or the refresh interval.
levels.2: Shows browse ETAs would need about 185,000 requests/s (9× the limit), 5 s refresh 111,000/s, 60 s refresh plus dispatch about 11,600/s (58%); uses Little's law for 555,600 active orders; checks the PSP at about 300/s.

levels.0: Endpoints named with no bodies, status codes or idempotency.
levels.1: Checkout and status endpoints with bodies, but no idempotency key, no repricing conflict, or no webhook.
levels.2: Browse with cursor and ETA ranges; POST /v1/orders with Idempotency-Key, quoted total and 409 on reprice; signed PSP webhook; versioned restaurant and courier commands returning 409 when stale; batched location upload; one WebSocket stream with versioned events.

levels.0: One database for everything, including every GPS ping.
levels.1: Separates positions from orders, but puts couriers and orders where assignment needs a cross-store lock.
levels.2: Postgres for orders, couriers, payments and outbox (one local transaction for assignment); Redis for live positions keyed by cell; derived cell lists and a search index fed by CDC; a unique (customer, idempotency key).

levels.0: A box diagram with no walkthrough.
levels.1: Walks checkout and dispatch, but location ingestion, browse or the event flow is missing.
levels.2: Walks browse (cell list, offline filter, internal ETA), checkout (one transaction with outbox, PSP intent, webhook), restaurant notification, dispatch and location/tracking separately, over a multi-AZ layout sized from the estimates.

levels.0: Charges the card inside the order request with no idempotency, or claims a distributed transaction with the PSP.
levels.1: Uses an idempotency key at the API but not at the PSP, or has no plan for webhooks that are duplicated or never arrive.
levels.2: Order row first; PSP intent keyed by order ID; conditional webhook transitions; sweeper querying the PSP and cancelling at a deadline; keyed refunds, including for late success on a cancelled order; daily reconciliation.

criteria.title: Order state machine across three parties

levels.0: A single linear status updated by whoever calls last.
levels.1: Versioned transitions, but kitchen and courier progress are forced into one sequence, or timers and cancellation races are not covered.
levels.2: Lifecycle state plus independent kitchen and courier sub-states; forward-only conditional updates that make commands idempotent; cancel-vs-pickup race decided by commit order; outbox with per-order ordering; timers stored as data.

levels.0: Picks the nearest courier with no protection against two orders taking the same courier.
levels.1: Uses a geo index and a lock or lease to avoid double-booking, but scores by distance only and has no batching rule.
levels.2: Cell-keyed geo index avoiding a per-city hot key; ETA matrix for top candidates scored against predicted food-ready time; windowed matching per city; batching with a cap on added delay; assignment as one conditional transaction with leases only for efficiency.

criteria.title: Location pipeline, tracking and restaurant reliability

levels.0: Writes every ping to the database and assumes restaurant tablets are always online.
levels.1: Keeps pings in memory and pushes tracking, but has no plan for an offline tablet or for the meal peaks.
levels.2: Stateless ingestion to Redis plus Kafka, push fan-out costed against polling; tablet heartbeats and ack timeouts, offline marking, phone escalation and auto-refund with a timeline; scheduled scale-out, shedding priorities and demand shaping.

levels.1: Covers zone and database loss, but not third-party outages, or not what breaks first at 10×.
levels.2: Zone loss with sized headroom, Postgres failover with idempotent retries, maps and PSP outages with fallbacks, dispatcher lease takeover; at 10× names the orders DB first, sharding by city to keep assignment local, and the maps limit forcing an internal ETA model.

levels.1: Generic trade-offs (SQL vs NoSQL, consistency vs availability) not tied to this design.
levels.2: Each key decision (couriers with orders in Postgres, positions in Redis, sub-states, outbox, windowed matching, conditional writes over locks, internal browse ETA, PSP intent keyed by order) comes with its alternative and the reason it lost here.
